# Draft:Georgian-Ayyubid wars

}}
The Georgian–Ayyubid wars were a series of conflicts fought between the Kingdom of Georgia and the Ayyubid Sultanate in eastern Anatolia between approximately 1208 and 1210. These wars formed part of the broader struggle for control over the Armenian Highlands and key strongholds such as Ahlat near Lake Van.
Background
During the late 12th and early 13th centuries, the Kingdom of Georgia reached the height of its power under Queen Tamar, expanding into Armenia and eastern Anatolia. At the same time, the Ayyubid dynasty, founded by Saladin, was consolidating power across the Near East following the decline of the Seljuk Empire.
In 1207, the Ayyubids took control of the former territories of the Shah-Armen dynasty, including the strategic city of Ahlat. This brought them into direct conflict with Georgian expansion into the same region.
The area was strategically important due to:
* Control of trade routes linking Anatolia, the Caucasus, and Iran
* Military access to frontier zones in Mesopotamia
* Influence over local Armenian principalities
Course of the wars
Georgian offensive
Around 1208, Georgian forces led by Ivane Mkhargrdzeli launched a campaign into eastern Anatolia, targeting Ahlat. The Georgians besieged the city in an attempt to secure dominance over the Armenian Highlands.
Ayyubid response
The Ayyubid ruler Al-Adil I organized a coalition army drawn from various emirates, including Homs, Hama, and Baalbek. This force advanced to relieve Ahlat and confront the Georgian army.
Capture of Ivane Mkhargrdzeli
During the campaign, Ivane Mkhargrdzeli was captured by Ayyubid forces near Ahlat. His capture significantly weakened the Georgian position and shifted the balance of power in favor of the Ayyubids.
Truce
Following negotiations, the Georgians agreed to a thirty-year truce in exchange for Ivane's release. This effectively ended the conflict around 1210.
Outcome
The war resulted in an Ayyubid strategic victory:
* Georgian expansion into eastern Anatolia was halted
* Ayyubid control over the Lake Van region was consolidated
* The Armenian Highlands remained divided between competing powers
Significance
The Georgian–Ayyubid wars marked the southern limit of Georgian expansion prior to the Mongol invasions of the 1220s, which would later transform the political landscape of the region.
The conflict also contributed to the stabilization of Ayyubid authority in eastern Anatolia and represents part of the wider pattern of Christian–Muslim frontier warfare during the High Middle Ages.
